newsitem.title: ITALY: Another Venetian separatist arrested in Italy.
newsitem.headline: Another Venetian separatist arrested in Italy.

text.p: Italian police on Monday said they had arrested another man after investigations into Venetian separatists who last week stormed the belltower in Venice's St Mark's Square demanding independence for the city.

Police said suspect Luigi Faccia was arrested on Saturday, the day after his brother and seven other armed men calling themselves the "Venetian Liberation Army" broke into the famous belltower to demand secession from Italy.
They were arrested after a five-hour stand-off and police immediately launched an inquiry across the region to see who else might have been behind the incident.

Faccia, 23, was arrested on suspicion of involvement in the armed group and with a string of recent interruptions to state television by someone who reads declarations of independence in the name of the "Most Serene Venetian Government".
Italian union leaders leading a demonstration in the square on Monday warned that the danger of separatists should not be underestimated.
"What happened here last Friday is a very serious act of real terrorism," Sergio Cofferati, head of the CGIL union, told the rally of about a thousand people.
"It would be best not to underestimate it," it said.
Cofferati harshly criticised a group of northern businessmen who have started a legal defence fund for the arrested men.
The group, known as The Free Federalist Entrepreneurs of Europe (LIFE), has accused the central government in Rome of strangling business entreprise in northeastern Italy with taxes and bureaucracy.
The LIFE group has opened an account at a bank in the city of Padua to receive contributions for the fund.
Police said 10 people had now been detained and a further 10 people questioned following Friday's incident.
Earlier on Monday, investigators said they had found a second home-made armoured vehicle similar to the one used by the separatists in their bizarre assault on the belltower.
The second vehicle was discovered near the northeastern town of Padua, some 40km (25 miles) from Venice, and almost certainly belonged to the same group, they said.
On Monday, the 200th anniversary of the demise of the Venetian Republic, an unidentified man phoned an Italian news agency in the northern city of Bologna to threaten further armed action.
"Glory to the heroes of the republic. We have struck and will strike again," the man said.

Venice, a centuries-old independent power known as the "Most Serene" republic, ruled an area stretching down the Adriatic and into the Middle East before falling in 1797 to French forces entering the city under Napoleon Bonaparte.
